Why use a feature branch for a database change?
column2:
To isolate work until it is ready for review and integration.
Start from main and merge the completed change through a pull request.
Review source

column1: In a feature-branch workflow, what state must main maintain?
column2:
It must remain deployable.
Use reviewed changes and build checks to reduce broken changes reaching main.
Review source

column1: Why keep database feature branches short-lived?
column2:
To reduce divergence and the difficulty of merging changes.
Integrate completed, reviewed work promptly rather than accumulating unrelated changes.
Review source

column1: What is the role of a pull request in the database change workflow?
column2:
Review and validate proposed changes before merging them into main.
Review the changed T-SQL and its consistency with project naming conventions.
Review source

column1: What compatibility risk must reviewers consider when a database column changes?
column2:
Existing queries or stored procedures can depend on its old definition.
Review affected consumers rather than judging only the edited table file.
Review source

column1: What must reviewers assess before approving a potentially destructive schema change?
column2:
Possible data loss and any required data migration.
A successful project build alone does not establish that production data will be preserved.
Review source

column1: Which deployment code needs review when a schema change affects required lookup values?
column2:
The corresponding post-deployment reference data scripts.
Keep the schema and the values needed by the application consistent.
Review source

column1: Which GitHub branch-protection setting gates merging on the SQL build check?
column2:
Require status checks to pass before merging.
Select a required check that actually builds the project. A skipped check can satisfy this rule.
Review source

column1: What causes a Git merge conflict in a SQL object definition?
column2:
Git cannot automatically reconcile the competing edits.
For example, both branches can change the same part of a CREATE TABLE statement.
Review source

column1: How do you resolve conflicting additions of different columns to one CREATE TABLE definition?
column2:
Combine both intended additions into one valid definition and remove the conflict markers.
Review column definitions and separators rather than blindly accepting either entire version.
Review source

column1: Why rebuild the SQL project after merging branches, even without text conflicts?
column2:
A clean text merge can still introduce broken references between objects.
For example, a merged procedure can reference a column that another branch renamed.
Review source

column1: How can you protect unfinished local work before starting a Git merge?
column2:
Commit or stash the local changes first.
Aborting a conflicted merge cannot always reconstruct uncommitted changes that existed before it started.
Review source

column1: Which Azure Repos branch policy requires a specified number of pull request approvals?
column2:
Require a minimum number of reviewers.
Meeting this count does not bypass other required branch policies.
Review source

column1: Which Azure Repos reviewer option excludes approval by the person who pushed the latest changes?
column2:
Prohibit the most recent pusher from approving their own changes.
The most recent pusher's approval does not count toward the policy.
Review source

column1: Which Azure Repos option clears approvals after a new push but preserves reject and wait votes?
column2:
Reset all approval votes (does not reset votes to reject or wait).
This prevents earlier approvals from covering newly pushed changes.
Review source

column1: How can Azure Repos require database-team review only for changes under a SQL project path?
column2:
Use an Automatically included reviewers policy set to Required with a matching path filter.
The filter limits the policy to changes in the selected files.
Review source
